probes.question: Doubling the grains on each of 64 squares, starting from 1, adds up to roughly...
True or false: the 64th square alone would hold more grains than the first 32 squares combined.

image.alt: Flat illustration of a chessboard with dots growing from tiny to large across the squares.

panels.text: In one old tale, the inventor of chess is offered a reward by his ruler. His request sounds modest: one grain of wheat on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, and so on, doubling each time.
The ruler laughs it off as a meager prize for a brilliant invention. The story is first known to have been recorded in 1256 by Ibn Khallikan.
But doubling is sneaky. By the fifth square the board holds just 31 grains. The 64th square alone would need 9,223,372,036,854,775,808 grains.
All 64 squares together: 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains, about 1,199,000,000,000 metric tons of wheat. That is over 1,400 times the world's yearly wheat harvest.
